fields.title: The Letter to the Galatians
fields.subtitle: Pros Galatas, “To the Galatians”
fields.description: Paul’s most urgent letter, written in astonishment to churches he had founded, which were being persuaded that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God’s people. He tells his own story, from persecutor to apostle, and of the day he opposed Peter to his face at Antioch; argues from Abraham, who believed God, and from the cross, where Christ became a curse on our behalf; and declares a family in which there is no Jew or Greek, slave or free, male and female, but all are one in Christ Jesus. Then freedom that serves, the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit, and a closing word in Paul’s own large letters: “far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross.” The letter Luther called his own. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Galatians?
qa.answer: The ninth book of the New Testament, a short letter from the apostle Paul to the churches of Galatia, in what is now central Turkey. It answers teachers who were telling Gentile believers that they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people. Paul insists that a person is justified through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law, and that those who belong to Christ are free, led by the Spirit and called to serve one another in love.

qa.question: Who wrote Galatians, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, who names himself in the first verse and writes the closing lines in his own hand (6:11). Almost all scholars accept that he wrote it. Its date depends on which Galatia he meant. If the churches were in the south of the Roman province, founded on the journey of Acts 13–14, it may have been written around AD 48–49, making it perhaps his earliest letter. If they were in the old Celtic territory to the north, it was probably written in the mid-50s, not long before Romans.

qa.question: What was the problem in the Galatian churches?
qa.answer: After Paul left, other teachers arrived who taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, apparently to be counted among Abraham’s children, and who questioned whether Paul was a true apostle. Paul says they are turning the Galatians to “a different gospel”, though “there is no second gospel” (1:6–7). For him, adding circumcision as a condition of belonging meant that Christ was no longer enough: “if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing at all” (2:21).

qa.question: What does “justified by faith” mean in Galatians?
qa.answer: To be justified is to be declared in the right by God. In Galatians Paul says that “no one is justified by works of the law; a person is justified only through faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16), and he points to Abraham, who “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (3:6). Christians differ on some details, such as whether “works of the law” means good works in general or especially the marks that set Jews apart, like circumcision and food laws, and whether “faith in Christ” may also mean Christ’s own faithfulness; but all agree that our standing with God is his gift in Christ.

qa.question: What is the fruit of the Spirit?
qa.answer: The list in Galatians 5:22–23 of what the Holy Spirit produces in believers: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Paul sets it against “the works of the flesh”, and speaks of one fruit, not many, as if these nine qualities were a single harvest. Of them he says, “No law stands against things like these.”

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Freedom was Christ’s purpose when he set us free. So stand firm, and do not let yourselves be held again under a yoke of slavery.

— Galatians 5:1

Almost every letter Paul wrote opens, after the greeting, with thanks or praise to God. Galatians does not. Where the thanksgiving should be, Paul writes: “I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from God, who called you by the grace of Christ, and going over to a different gospel.”

It is the angriest of his letters, and one of the most loving. Paul is frightened for these churches, which he founded himself, and he writes with the urgency of a parent whose child has wandered toward a cliff. In six short chapters he tells his own story, argues from Scripture, pleads, scolds, jokes bitterly, and at the end takes the pen in his own hand to write in large letters. The question at stake seemed to some a small one: whether Gentile believers needed to be circumcised. Paul saw that the whole gospel hung on the answer.

The churches of Galatia and the crisis

Galatia was a region in the middle of what is now Turkey, named after Celtic tribes who settled there in the third century BC, and also the name of a larger Roman province reaching further south. Christians have long debated which Paul means. If he means the southern part of the province, the churches are those of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, which Acts says he founded with Barnabas (Acts 13–14), and the letter may be one of his earliest, written around AD 48–49. If he means the Celtic north, he founded the churches on a later journey (Acts 16:6; 18:23), and wrote perhaps in the mid-50s, not long before Romans. Good scholars hold both views.

What happened is clearer. After Paul left, other teachers came, Jewish believers in Jesus, who taught that Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God’s people, the children of Abraham. Paul calls them “some people who are unsettling you”. They seem also to have said that Paul was a second-hand apostle, dependent on Jerusalem, who had watered the gospel down to win Gentiles. Paul answers both charges.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapters 1–2: Paul’s gospel and Paul’s story. His call came straight from God, not from any human source; the leaders in Jerusalem recognised it; and at Antioch he defended it even against Peter.
  • Chapters 3–4: the argument from Scripture. The Spirit received by faith; Abraham; the curse of the law and the cross; the law as a guardian until Christ; children and heirs; and Hagar and Sarah.
  • Chapters 5–6: the life of freedom. Freedom not to be lost, not to be abused; the flesh and the Spirit; bearing one another’s loads; the cross and the new creation.

An apostle from God

Paul begins by insisting that he was “sent not from any human source, nor through any human go-between”. He had been a zealous persecutor of the church. Then God, who had set him apart from birth, “chose to reveal his Son in me”. He did not go to Jerusalem to be taught. He went away to Arabia, then back to Damascus, and only three years later went to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas, that is Peter, staying fifteen days. Fourteen years later he went up again, with Barnabas and with Titus, an uncircumcised Greek believer. The leaders there, “James, Cephas and John, who were regarded as pillars”, added nothing to his message. They gave him the right hand of fellowship, and asked only that he “keep remembering the poor”.

Scholars differ on how this visit fits the story in Acts, whether it is the council of Acts 15 or the earlier famine visit of Acts 11:30. Either way, Paul’s point is that his gospel did not come from Jerusalem, and that Jerusalem recognised it.

Then comes the most dramatic scene in the letter. At Antioch, Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, until people came from James, and Peter, afraid, pulled back. Even Barnabas followed. Paul confronted him in front of everyone: “How then can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?” For Paul, a church that ate at separate tables was denying the gospel. Whether his words to Peter end in 2:14 or run on to the end of the chapter, the chapter ends in the gospel itself:

We ourselves are Jews by birth, not Gentile sinners. Yet we know that no one is justified by works of the law; a person is justified only through faith in Jesus Christ. So we too have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because no human being will be justified by works of the law.

— Galatians 2:15–16

And then, in the first person, its heart:

I am no longer the one who lives; Christ lives in me. Whatever life I still have in the flesh is a life lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for my sake.

— Galatians 2:20

Faith, the Spirit and Abraham

“You foolish Galatians! Who has put you under a spell?” Paul appeals first to their own experience. They had received the Spirit, and seen miracles, not by keeping the law but by believing the message. “You made your start by the Spirit; are you now going to reach the goal by the flesh?”

Then he turns to Abraham, the very figure the other teachers relied on. Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”, and God promised that in him all the nations would be blessed. So “the people of faith are the ones who are Abraham’s children”. Those who rely on the law, Paul argues, fall under its curse, because no one does everything it requires. But “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse on our behalf”, hanging on a tree, so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles.

What, then, was the law for? It came 430 years after the promise and cannot cancel it. It served as a guardian, the household slave who looked after a child until he came of age. And now that faith has come, a new family has been formed:

For in Christ Jesus you are all children of God, through faith. Every one of you who was baptized into Christ has put on Christ like clothing. There is no Jew or Greek, there is no slave or free person, there is no male and female, for all of you are one in Christ Jesus.

— Galatians 3:26–28

The old dividing lines of the ancient world, between Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female, do not decide who belongs to God’s family. Christians apply this verse in different ways, but no reading can make it say less than that all are equally heirs.

Children and heirs

Chapter 4 tells the same story as a family drama. An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave, until the date his father has set. “But when the time God had set was complete, God sent out his Son”, born of a woman and under the law, so that we might be adopted. The proof of adoption is the Spirit, who cries out in believers’ hearts, “Abba, Father!”, the word Jesus himself used. Why would they go back to slavery?

Then Paul speaks more personally. When he first came to them he was ill, and they welcomed him “like an angel of God, like Christ Jesus himself”; they would have given him their own eyes. Now he is suffering birth pains over them again, “until Christ is formed in you.” The chapter ends with an allegory of Abraham’s two sons, one born of Hagar the slave woman and one of Sarah the free woman, which Paul reads as two covenants: “we are children not of a slave woman but of the free woman.”

Freedom, flesh and Spirit

Chapter 5 begins with the letter’s battle cry and its warning. If they accept circumcision as the way to be justified, they have cut themselves off from Christ. “What counts is faith at work through love.” In his anger at the teachers, Paul uses words as coarse as any he wrote, wishing they would go the whole way and castrate themselves.

But freedom is not licence. “Only do not let your freedom become an opening for the flesh. Instead, through love, be slaves to one another.” The whole law is summed up in one sentence: “You must love your neighbor as you love yourself.” Where the law could not make people good, the Spirit can. Paul sets the works of the flesh, a grim list from sexual immorality to drunken bouts, beside a single harvest:

But the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. No law stands against things like these.

— Galatians 5:22–23

Notice that it is fruit, not fruits: one life of the Spirit, showing itself in nine ways. Chapter 6 turns it into practice. Restore the one who falls, gently. “Take up one another’s heavy loads, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” Do not tire of doing good.

In Paul’s own hand

At the end Paul takes the pen from his secretary. “Notice what large letters I make as I write to you in my own hand.” Perhaps it was for emphasis; perhaps his eyesight was poor. And in those large letters he writes the letter’s summary: the other teachers want to boast in the Galatians’ flesh, “but far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” What matters is not circumcision or uncircumcision but “a new creation.”

Galatians in the life of the church

Martin Luther lectured on Galatians twice, and his great commentary on it, from lectures of 1531, became one of the most influential books of the Reformation. He said that Galatians was his own epistle, to which he was betrothed: “my Katie von Bora”, after his wife.

More than a century later, John Bunyan, in despair over his sins, found an old copy of that commentary, “so old that it was ready to fall piece from piece”. He wrote in Grace Abounding that he preferred it, after the Bible, to all the books he had ever seen, “as most fit for a wounded conscience.” And in May 1738 Charles Wesley was reading Luther on Galatians in the days before his own assurance of faith, which came on Pentecost Sunday, three days before his brother John’s at Aldersgate.

How to read Galatians

Galatians can be read in half an hour, and should be, aloud and at a sitting, so that the heat of it comes through. Then go back and follow the argument: Paul’s story in chapters 1 and 2, the Scriptures in 3 and 4, the life of freedom in 5 and 6. Notice how each part answers the same question, whether faith in Christ is enough. And notice that the most fiercely argued letter in the New Testament ends with love, the fruit of the Spirit, and bearing each other’s burdens.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Galatians are worth knowing about before you begin.

“Faith in Jesus Christ.” In 2:16 and 3:22 the Greek says literally “faith of Jesus Christ”, and in 2:20 “faith of the Son of God”. It can mean faith that has Christ as its object, or Christ’s own faithfulness to God. This translation follows the first reading, and its notes give the second, which many scholars hold.

“Justified.” In Galatians the translation keeps the familiar word “justified” for God’s verdict that a person is in the right with him, and “righteousness” for the related noun, so that a reader can follow the argument from 2:16 to 5:5.

“Children of God.” In 3:26 and 4:5–7 Paul’s word is “sons”, the standing of a son and heir in the ancient world, which he gives to women and men alike. This edition prints “children”; the Open Word Bible lets a reader choose “sons” instead, which keeps the link to the Son whom God sent. In the same way it prints “brothers and sisters” where the Greek word is masculine in form but Paul addresses the whole church.

“The elemental forces of the world.” In 4:3 and 4:9 Paul uses a word that can mean the basic elements of the world, the first principles of religion, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. This translation chooses a phrase broad enough to hold more than one of these.

“The Israel of God.” In the closing blessing (6:16) it is uncertain whether Paul means the whole church, Jewish and Gentile believers together, Jewish believers in particular, or the people of Israel. The translation leaves the phrase as it stands, and Christians read it in all three ways.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Galatians 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, an apostle sent not from any human source, nor through any human go-between, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and from all the brothers and sisters who are with me, to the churches of Galatia. Grace and peace to you from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age, as our God and Father willed. To him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

There is no other gospel

I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from God, who called you by the grace of Christ, and going over to a different gospel. But there is no second gospel. There are only some people who are unsettling you and want to twist the gospel of Christ into something else. But even if we ourselves, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than the one we preached to you, let that one be under God’s curse. We have said it before, and now I say it again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel other than the one you received, let that one be under God’s curse.

Is it people I am trying to win over now, or God? Or is my aim to please people? If I were still out to please people, I would be no servant of Christ.

Paul’s gospel came from God, not from people

For I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that the gospel I preached is no human invention. I did not receive it from any human being, and nobody taught it to me. It came to me through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

You have heard about the way I once lived in Judaism: how fiercely I persecuted God’s church and set out to destroy it. I was moving ahead in Judaism faster than many people my age among my own people, because I was far more zealous for the traditions handed down from my ancestors. But God set me apart from birth and called me by his grace, and when he chose to reveal his Son in me so that I would proclaim the gospel about him among the Gentiles, I did not at once turn to any human being for advice. I did not go up to Jerusalem to see those who were apostles before me. Instead I went away to Arabia, and afterward I came back to Damascus.

Paul’s first visit to Jerusalem

Three years later I did go up to Jerusalem, to get to know Cephas, and I stayed with him for fifteen days. Apart from James, the Lord’s brother, I did not see any of the other apostles. Now, as God sees me, I am not lying in what I write to you. After that I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. The churches of Judea that are in Christ still did not know me by sight. They only kept hearing it said, “The man who used to persecute us is now proclaiming the faith he once set out to destroy.” And because of me they glorified God.

fields.title: Galatians 2
fields.body_html:
The leaders in Jerusalem accept Paul

Then, fourteen years later, I went up to Jerusalem again, this time with Barnabas, and I took Titus along as well. I went up because God had shown me that I should. I set out before them the gospel I proclaim among the Gentiles, though I did this privately, with those who were regarded as leaders. I did not want to find that I was running, or had run, for nothing. Yet not even Titus, who was with me, was forced to be circumcised, though he was a Greek. This came up because of false brothers who had been smuggled in. They slipped in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus, so that they could make us slaves. We did not give in to them, not even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you. As for those who were regarded as important (what they once were makes no difference to me, since God is not swayed by a person’s standing), those leaders added nothing to my message. On the contrary, they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised. For God, who was at work in Peter to make him an apostle to the circumcised, was also at work in me for the Gentiles. James, Cephas and John, who were regarded as pillars, recognized the grace that had been given to me, and they gave Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship. We agreed that we would go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. They asked only that we keep remembering the poor, and that is the very thing I was eager to do.

Paul opposes Cephas at Antioch

But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him face to face, because he was clearly in the wrong. Before some people came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But once they had come, he started to pull back and hold himself apart, afraid of those who insisted on circumcision. The other Jewish believers joined in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was swept along by their pretense. But when I saw that they were not walking in step with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas in front of them all, “You are a Jew, yet you live like a Gentile and not like a Jew. How then can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?” We ourselves are Jews by birth, not Gentile sinners. Yet we know that no one is justified by works of the law; a person is justified only through faith in Jesus Christ. So we too have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because no human being will be justified by works of the law. But if, while we seek to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners too, does that make Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not! For if I rebuild what I tore down, I show that I am a lawbreaker. For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live for God. I have been crucified with Christ. I am no longer the one who lives; Christ lives in me. Whatever life I still have in the flesh is a life lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and handed himself over for my sake. I do not cancel out God’s grace. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing at all.

fields.title: Galatians 3
fields.body_html:
Faith or works of the law?

You foolish Galatians! Who has put you under a spell? Jesus Christ was set out in full view before your eyes as the crucified one. Tell me just this one thing: did you receive the Spirit by works of the law, or by faith in what you heard? Are you really that foolish? You made your start by the Spirit; are you now going to reach the goal by the flesh? Did you go through so much for nothing? If it really was for nothing. So then, does God give you the Spirit and work miracles among you because of works of the law, or because of faith in what you heard? So it was with Abraham: he believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.

Abraham’s children by faith

You can see, then, that the people of faith are the ones who are Abraham’s children. Scripture saw in advance that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and so it announced the gospel ahead of time to Abraham: “In you all the nations will be blessed.” So the people of faith share in the blessing together with Abraham, who believed.

Christ set us free from the curse

For everyone whose standing rests on works of the law is under a curse. Scripture says, “A curse is on everyone who does not hold fast to everything written in the book of the law and do it.” It is plain that no one is justified in God’s sight through the law, since “The one who is righteous will live by faith.” But the law does not rest on faith. Instead, “Whoever does these things will live by them.” Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse on our behalf, for it is written, “A curse is on everyone who is hung on a tree.” He did this so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham would reach the Gentiles, and so that through faith we would receive the Spirit who was promised.

The law cannot cancel the promise

Brothers and sisters, I will use an illustration from human life. Even a human will, once it has been made binding, is something no one can cancel or add new terms to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his descendant. Notice that Scripture does not say “and to descendants,” as if many people were meant. It speaks of one: “and to your descendant,” and that one is Christ. My point is this. God had already ratified a covenant, and the law, coming 430 years afterward, cannot overturn it and so cancel the promise. For if the inheritance depends on the law, it no longer depends on a promise. But God gave it freely to Abraham by means of a promise.

Why the law was given

What, then, was the law for? It was added because of transgressions, and only until the offspring should come, the one to whom the promise was made. Angels set it in order, and it came through the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator does not act for one party alone, but God is one.

Does the law, then, oppose God’s promises? Certainly not! Had any law been given with the power to make people alive, then righteousness would in fact come by way of the law. But Scripture has locked up everything under the power of sin, so that what was promised might be given, on the ground of faith in Jesus Christ, to those who believe.

No longer under a guardian

Until faith came, the law held us in custody. We were kept shut in, waiting for the faith that was going to be revealed. In this way the law served as our guardian until the coming of Christ, so that faith would be the way we are justified. Faith has now come, and we are no longer in the care of a guardian. For in Christ Jesus you are all children of God, through faith. Every one of you who was baptized into Christ has put on Christ like clothing. There is no Jew or Greek, there is no slave or free person, there is no male and female, for all of you are one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, it follows that you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs in keeping with the promise.

fields.title: Galatians 4
fields.body_html:
No longer slaves but heirs

Here is what I mean. While the heir is still a child, his position is no better than a slave’s, even though he is master of everything. Guardians and managers have charge of him until the date his father has set. In the same way we too, when we were children, were held as slaves under the elemental forces of the world. But when the time God had set was complete, God sent out his Son. He was born of a woman and born under the law, to redeem those who lived under the law, so that we might be adopted as children. And since you are children, God has sent out the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, and the Spirit cries, “Abba, Father!” So you are no longer a slave but a child, and if you are a child, then you are also an heir, made so by God.

Why turn back to slavery?

In the past you did not know God, and you were slaves to beings that are not gods by nature. But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you go back to those weak and worthless elemental forces and want to serve them as slaves once more? You keep special days and months, seasons and years. I am afraid for you. I fear that the work I did for you may have been wasted.

Paul pleads with the Galatians

Be as I am, brothers and sisters, I beg you, since I made myself as you were. You did me no wrong. You know that I preached the gospel to you the first time because of a weakness of the flesh. And though my flesh was a trial to you, you did not scorn me or spit in disgust. No, you received me like an angel of God, like Christ Jesus himself. What has become, then, of the way you once counted yourselves blessed? I can vouch for you: you would have gouged out your own eyes and handed them to me if that had been possible. So is it the truth I tell you that has made me your enemy? These people pay you eager attention, but their motives are not good. They want to shut you out, so that you will pay eager attention to them. It is always good to be sought after for a good purpose, and not only when I am there with you. My children, I am suffering birth pains over you a second time, and I will until Christ is formed in you. I would like to be there with you now and speak in another tone, for I do not know what to make of you.

Hagar and Sarah: two covenants

You who want to be under the law, tell me: do you not hear what the law says? Scripture says that Abraham had two sons: one was the son of the slave woman, the other the son of the free woman. The slave woman’s son was born according to the flesh, but the free woman’s son was born through the promise. These things can be read as an allegory. The two women are two covenants. One comes from Mount Sinai and bears children who will be slaves; this is Hagar. Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia, and she matches the Jerusalem of the present time, since she is in slavery together with her children. The Jerusalem above, however, is free, and it is she who is our mother. For it is written: “Be glad, barren woman, you who have borne no child; break into a shout, you who have never been in labor. For the woman left alone has many children, more than the woman who has a husband.” And you, brothers and sisters, are children of the promise, as Isaac was. In those days the son born according to the flesh persecuted the son born according to the Spirit, and it is the same now. But what does Scripture say? “Send away the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share the inheritance with the free woman’s son.” So then, brothers and sisters, we are children not of a slave woman but of the free woman.

fields.title: Galatians 5
fields.body_html:
Stand firm in your freedom

Freedom was Christ’s purpose when he set us free. So stand firm, and do not let yourselves be held again under a yoke of slavery.

Listen! I, Paul, am telling you: if you have yourselves circumcised, Christ will do you no good at all. I insist once more to every man who has himself circumcised: he puts himself under obligation to carry out the entire law. Any of you who look to the law to justify you have been cut off from Christ; you have fallen away from grace. But we, by the Spirit and on the ground of faith, are eagerly waiting for the righteousness we hope for. For in Christ Jesus, being circumcised or uncircumcised counts for nothing. What counts is faith at work through love.

Who blocked your way?

You had been running a good race. Who got in your way and turned you from obeying the truth? That persuasion did not come from the one who calls you. A little yeast spreads through all the dough. In the Lord I am confident that you will not think otherwise. But the one who is unsettling you will bear God’s judgment, whoever that may be. As for me, brothers and sisters, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the cross would have stopped being a stumbling block. As for those who are stirring you up, I wish they would go the whole way and castrate themselves!

Free to serve one another in love

You were called to be free, brothers and sisters. Only do not let your freedom become an opening for the flesh. Instead, through love, be slaves to one another. The whole law comes to its fullness in one sentence: “You must love your neighbor as you love yourself.” But if you keep biting one another and tearing each other apart, be careful, or you will end up destroying one another.

Walk by the Spirit

This is what I mean: walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out what the flesh desires. For the flesh sets its desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. They are at war with each other, so that you are not free to do whatever you please. But if the Spirit is leading you, you are not under the law. The works of the flesh are plain to see: sexual immorality, impurity, indecency, idolatry, sorcery, hostility, quarreling, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish rivalry, divisions, factions, envy, drunken bouts, wild partying, and other things like these. I am telling you now, as I told you before: people who live this way will not inherit the kingdom of God.

But the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. No law stands against things like these. Those who belong to Christ have nailed the flesh to the cross, together with its passions and desires. Since our life comes from the Spirit, let us also follow the Spirit’s lead in each step we take. We must not become people hungry for empty praise, who challenge one another and envy one another.

fields.title: Galatians 6
fields.body_html:
Carry one another’s burdens

Brothers and sisters, suppose someone is caught out in some wrongdoing. You who are spiritual must set that person right again, and do it with a gentle spirit. Keep an eye on yourself as you do, in case you are tempted too. Take up one another’s heavy loads, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For those who think they are something when they are nothing are only fooling themselves. Each of you should examine your own conduct. Then any pride you take will be in what you yourself have done, not in how you compare with someone else. For each of you will have your own load to carry.

You will reap what you sow

Those who are being taught the word must share all their good things with the one who teaches them. Do not let anyone mislead you: God is not to be sneered at. Whatever people sow, that is what they will reap. Those who sow into their own flesh will gather a harvest of decay from the flesh; those who sow into the Spirit will gather from the Spirit a harvest of eternal life. We must not tire of doing good. When the right time comes we will bring in the harvest, as long as we do not slacken. So whenever we have the chance, we should do good to everyone, and above all to those who belong to the family of faith.

Paul’s last words in his own hand

Notice what large letters I make as I write to you in my own hand. The people who want to make a fine impression in the flesh are the ones pressing you to be circumcised. They have one motive: they do not want to suffer persecution because of the cross of Christ. For even these circumcised people do not themselves obey the law. What they want is your circumcision, so that your flesh can be something for them to boast about. But far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Through that cross the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; the one thing that matters is a new creation. May peace and mercy be on all who live in line with this rule, and on the Israel of God.

Let no one give me any more trouble from now on, for I carry on my body the marks that show I belong to Jesus.

Brothers and sisters, may the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
But far be it from me to boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Through that cross the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

— Galatians 6:14

Galatians ends where it began, at the cross. In the first chapter Christ “gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age”; in the last, Paul will boast of nothing else. Everything between, his story, his quarrel with Peter, Abraham, the law, Hagar and Sarah, the flesh and the Spirit, is an argument that the cross is enough.

The question the letter leaves

The Galatians were not tempted to give up Christ. They were tempted to add something to him: a mark in the flesh, a calendar of holy days, a way of proving that they really belonged. Paul’s question to them is the one the letter leaves with every reader: is Christ enough, or is he only the start? “You made your start by the Spirit; are you now going to reach the goal by the flesh?”

The temptation takes new forms in every age, and not all of them are religious. Whatever we lean on to make ourselves acceptable, to God or to others, Galatians names it a yoke of slavery. And it does not answer with a new set of rules, but with a person: “Christ lives in me.”

Where the letter points

It points to freedom, and to a freedom that serves. The same chapter that cries “stand firm” also says “through love, be slaves to one another.” Paul does not trade law for licence. He trades life under the law for life in the Spirit, whose fruit is love, joy, peace and the rest: “No law stands against things like these.”

And it points to one family. At Antioch the gospel was at stake around a dinner table, and in Galatia around who could be counted Abraham’s children. Paul’s answer was that all who belong to Christ are heirs together, “one in Christ Jesus”, Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female. A church that lives by faith eats at one table.

Where to go from here

Galatians has set more than one heart free, and a number of the people it reached are in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On freedom. Martin Luther’s Concerning Christian Liberty, in First Principles of the Reformation, and The Key Teachings of Martin Luther, whose chapters on law and gospel and on the freedom of a Christian follow the man who called this letter his own.
  • On grace for a wounded conscience. John Bunyan’s Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, with his account of finding Luther on Galatians.
  • On being crucified with Christ (2:20). Elisabeth Elliot’s Christ Lives in Me, A. W. Tozer’s I Am Crucified with Christ and A. B. Simpson’s The Death of Self.
  • On faith at work through love (5:6). Catherine Booth’s A True and a False Faith.
  • On the Spirit. In Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, the New Testament volume, the chapter “The Holy Spirit in Galatians”.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Galatians in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

Then read Romans, where Paul, calmer and at greater length, takes up the same questions of faith, law, Abraham and the Spirit. Galatians is the battle; Romans is the account written afterwards. But it may be best first to read this letter again, at a sitting, and to hear, under the anger, a man who cannot bear to see anyone lose the freedom Christ has won. His last encouragement is for every reader who has grown weary:

We must not tire of doing good. When the right time comes we will bring in the harvest, as long as we do not slacken.

— Galatians 6:9
